sections.title: Build mvnex from source
sections.description: mvnex does not have an official Homebrew, winget, or packaged release yet. The current way to use it is to clone the repository and build the native CLI locally.
sections.intro: This guide walks through the source-based workflow used today. It is useful for trying mvnex before packaged releases exist, testing local changes, or contributing to the CLI.
requirements: CMake, to configure and generate the build files.
A C++ compiler supported by your platform.
Maven or Maven Wrapper support for building generated projects.

blocks.title: Run mvnex
blocks.description: Use the local binary to create a Maven project.

notes: The binary lives in the local build directory.
Commands shown in the docs assume mvnex is available on your PATH. When running from source, use ./build/mvnex or add the build output to PATH manually.
Packaged installation commands will be documented separately once official releases exist.

sections.title: Create a Maven project
sections.description: mvnex init creates a standard Maven project and protects the boring setup details: naming, package paths, Java version, wrapper files, and a first source entry point.
sections.intro: You can run it interactively when exploring, or pass flags when you already know the configuration. Either way, the output is a normal Maven project.
requirements: Project name, used for the directory and generated artifactId.
Maven groupId, used for package generation and pom.xml metadata.
Java version, written into the generated Maven configuration.
Whether Maven Wrapper files should be generated.

output.title: What mvnex creates.
output.description: A project generated by mvnex is still a normal Maven project. The generated files are meant to be readable by Maven, IDEs, CI systems, and developers who never install mvnex.
output.intro: This page explains the scaffold created by mvnex init, why each file exists, and how to verify the project after generation.

notes: The exact Java package path depends on the groupId, artifactId, and optional --package value selected during init.
Wrapper files are present by default. If you create the project with --no-wrapper, mvnw, mvnw.cmd, and .mvn/wrapper are omitted.
The generated output intentionally stays close to standard Maven conventions, so build tools and IDEs do not need mvnex-specific support.

details.name: pom.xml
details.description: The Maven source of truth. It contains the selected groupId, artifactId, version, Java compiler settings, and the baseline project metadata.

details.name: src/main/java
details.description: The production source tree. mvnex creates the package folder and starter Java class here.

details.name: src/test/java
details.description: The test source tree. It mirrors the package layout so tests can be added without changing the Maven structure later.

details.name: .mvn/wrapper
details.description: Maven Wrapper configuration. It pins how the wrapper downloads and runs Maven for this project.

details.name: mvnw
details.description: Unix/macOS wrapper script. Use it when Maven is not installed globally or when CI should use the project wrapper.

details.name: mvnw.cmd
details.description: Windows wrapper script with the same purpose as mvnw, but for Command Prompt and PowerShell workflows.

behavior: The generated pom.xml is authoritative. mvnex does not keep hidden project state somewhere else.
The package path is derived from the selected Java package, not from a custom mvnex format.
When wrapper generation is enabled, users can run the project without installing Maven globally.
When wrapper generation is disabled, the project expects mvn to be available on PATH.
You can edit the generated project like any other Maven project after creation.

principles.title: Maven stays Maven.
principles.description: mvnex is designed as a helper around standard Maven projects, not as a new project format or hidden build system.
principles.intro: These principles guide which features belong in mvnex, how generated projects should behave, and how the CLI should evolve without making Java projects harder to understand.

details.name: pom.xml is authoritative
details.description: Project metadata, dependencies, plugins, packaging, and compiler settings live in pom.xml. mvnex can edit or generate that file, but it should not move truth into a private config format.

details.name: Maven lifecycle remains intact
details.description: Generated projects must keep working with normal Maven commands such as mvn compile, mvn test, and mvn package.

details.name: No lock-in
details.description: A developer should be able to delete mvnex and continue working on the generated project with Maven, an IDE, or CI.

details.name: Commands reduce friction
details.description: A command belongs in mvnex only when it removes repetitive setup or makes a common Maven workflow clearer.

details.name: Generated output is readable
details.description: The files created by mvnex should look familiar to Java developers. There should be no surprising generated structure that only mvnex understands.

details.name: Interactive when useful
details.description: Prompts should help users make choices, but flags should exist for scripts, CI, and developers who already know the values they want.

behavior: mvnex init creates a standard Maven project instead of a mvnex-specific workspace.
Maven Wrapper is generated to improve portability, not to replace Maven itself.
Future dependency commands should update pom.xml directly and leave it understandable.
Future install paths should make mvnex easier to get, while generated projects remain independent from the installer.
Documentation should explain the Maven result, not only the mvnex command that produced it.

roadmap.title: Where mvnex goes next.
roadmap.description: The current documentation reflects the source-based workflow and the init command. The roadmap shows the areas that should become first-class once the CLI grows.
roadmap.intro: The order is intentionally practical: make mvnex easy to install, make project creation solid, then expand into the Maven workflows that create repeated friction.

details.name: Package-manager install
details.description: Document official Homebrew support for macOS and an equivalent Windows path when those releases exist. Until then, Build from source remains the source of truth.

details.name: Dependency workflows
details.description: Add focused pages for adding, removing, inspecting, and updating dependencies while keeping pom.xml readable and authoritative.

details.name: Command reference
details.description: Give every command its own page with synopsis, flags, defaults, examples, generated changes, and copyable commands.

details.name: Configuration reference
details.description: If mvnex gains user or project configuration, document the file format, precedence rules, defaults, and migration behavior.

details.name: Release notes
details.description: Track changes that affect commands, generated project structure, install paths, and compatibility expectations.

details.name: Contribution guide
details.description: Explain how to build mvnex locally, run checks, test generated Maven projects, and propose new command behavior.

roadmap.behaviorTitle: Documentation rules while the project grows
behavior: Do not document Homebrew, winget, or packaged installs as available until they actually exist.
Keep source-based usage visible while mvnex is still distributed from the repository.
When a command becomes available, move it from planned workflow to its own command page.
Each new page should exist in English and Spanish with equivalent structure.
Examples should prefer real commands users can copy and run.

interactive: When you run mvnex init without enough flags, mvnex opens a guided prompt instead of guessing silently.
It asks for the project name when it was not provided as a positional argument.
It proposes defaults for groupId, package name, Java version, and Maven Wrapper generation before writing files.
Each answer is validated immediately, so invalid Maven coordinates, Java package names, or unsupported Java versions are caught before the project is created.
At the end of the flow, mvnex creates the directory, writes pom.xml, creates the Java source and test folders, and adds wrapper files unless --no-wrapper was selected.
